lab_title: AR Lab: Apparent Retrograde Motion of Mars
top_level_objectives: Describe and quantify apparent retrograde motion as seen from Earth
Explain how heliocentric orbital motion and relative speed produce retrograde loops
Compare retrograde signatures for Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn and relate loop size to orbital radius and relative speed
Connect observational evidence of retrograde motion to the historical shift from geocentric to heliocentric models

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the phenomenon by showing Mars embedded in the familiar star field and motivating the puzzle: why would a planet ever reverse?
key_visuals: Realistic night-sky dome with constellations along the ecliptic
A bright red Mars marker among stars
Quick overlay text: 'Mars usually moves east — but sometimes it loops'
student_actions: Look around the sky dome and tap the Mars marker to hear a short prompt question about reversal
Read a one-sentence challenge: 'Can you explain why Mars sometimes moves backward?']},{

scene_name":"2. Nightly Earth-surface Time Series","brief_purpose":"Let students observe Mars' path against background stars across consecutive nights to see a full retrograde loop form","key_visuals":["Sequence of 30-60 translucent nightly position markers forming a path across constellations","Calendar strip showing dates (night numbers) and a slider to scrub nights","Local horizon and a simple ground avatar to indicate Earth-surface viewpoint"],"student_actions":["Play a night-by-night animation or manually scrub the date slider to trace Mars' motion","Tap nightly markers to reveal date labels and small glyphs of east/west movement","Use an on-screen tool to measure angular displacement between selected nights and note the interval when eastward motion turns westward"]},{

scene_name":"3. Quantify the Loop","brief_purpose":"Have students extract simple measurements (angular speed, direction change, loop width) to characterize the retrograde event","key_visuals":["Highlighted segment of the path showing the retrograde loop with start/end points","Vector arrows indicating instantaneous nightly motion and a small inset graph plotting RA (or ecliptic longitude) vs. time","A measurement tool UI with readouts for angular displacement per night and total loop span"],"student_actions":["Select three nights to calculate nightly angular speeds and record values","Use the measurement tool to compute total loop angular width and duration","Answer a short prompt comparing measured speeds before, during, and after retrograde"]},{

scene_name":"4. External Heliocentric View — Relative Motion","brief_purpose":"Switch perspective to a view outside the solar system showing Earth and Mars orbiting the Sun so students can link the observed loop to relative motion and overtaking","key_visuals":["Sun at center, scaled (not to real scale) circular or slightly elliptical orbits for Earth and Mars with labeled orbital radii","Markers showing Earth and Mars positions at the same dates previously observed, with a camera line-of-sight back to Earth showing the apparent sky position","Velocity vectors on Earth and Mars arrows showing faster Earth speed","A 'play' time-lapse control to run the same date range as Scene 2"] ,"student_actions":["Play the heliocentric time-lapse while watching the camera-line-of-sight projection trace Mars' apparent sky path
Drag Earth forward through its orbit to 'pass' Mars and observe how the projection loops
Explain in one or two sentences how overtaking produces an apparent backward motion

scenes.brief_purpose: Have students compare the retrograde signature of Mars with Jupiter and Saturn to see how orbital distance affects loop size and duration
key_visuals: Three overlaid orbital systems (Earth+Mars, Earth+Jupiter, Earth+Saturn) selectable via tabs
Side-by-side sky-path overlays showing loops scaled to angular size as seen from Earth
Numeric readouts: relative orbital periods, ratio of speeds, predicted loop angular spans
student_actions: Select Jupiter and Saturn in turn and run the time-lapse to view their loops
Record and compare loop width and duration for each planet using a quick 'compare' table
Predict which planet will show the largest apparent loop and justify the answer using relative speed and distance

scenes.brief_purpose: Conclude by asking students to synthesize observations with historical models and assess which model explains retrograde motion more simply
key_visuals: Split-screen: geocentric sketch with epicycles vs. heliocentric orbit schematic
A brief timeline card referencing Ptolemy and Copernicus with a highlight on observational fit
A final checklist of takeaways (overtaking, loop size, predictive simplicity)
student_actions: Choose which model (geocentric with epicycles or heliocentric) better explains the observed loops and drag in supporting evidence from earlier measurements
Complete a short multiple-choice question and a one-sentence summary explaining why the heliocentric model is preferred based on retrograde motion
